summary: BG2 episode recorded on Liberation Day: tariffs and market reaction, China open source and DeepSeek vs OpenAI open weights, OpenAI valuation and unit economics, CoreWeave IPO and GPU depreciation, TikTok deal. Conclusions: tariffs will land lower than announced after negotiation, buy fear selectively, models commoditize and value moves to products.

coverage.note: agenda, market reaction to Liberation Day, non-tariff barriers
free-trade theory, reshoring, uncertainty and capex
cascading effects, Nasdaq drawdown, forecast tariffs, buying fear
mega-round promo, unit economics, losses, Uber analogy
ChatGPT metrics, compute demand, toy thesis
CoreWeave customer mix, IPO timing, business model
IPO delays, GPU depreciation, CoreWeave economics
GPU lifetimes, depreciation pushback, Nvidia multiple, IPO price

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: You know this was doctrinal.
claims.claim: The administration's tariff push is a philosophical, doctrinal belief about fair trade rather than just a bargaining ploy; the debate is only how big, so conservative positioning was warranted.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: pro business pro investment lower taxes less regulation pro M&A
claims.claim: The pro-growth agenda (lower taxes, less regulation, M&A flywheel, AI super cycle) is the bullish side; the open question is how large tariffs land and how budget cuts offset.
claims.conditions: Bullish if tariffs land at the low end

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: They had a 600 basis point fall between where they initially jumped and where they ended up.
claims.claim: Markets rose ~2.5% on a 10% across-the-board headline, then futures fell sharply when the reciprocal tariff table (China 54%) was shown; indices were already down 8-15% YTD.
claims.indicator: S&P and Nasdaq futures on tariff headline

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: they call them non-tariff trade barriers. This is everything from what they call currency manipulation
claims.claim: Reciprocal tariffs are calculated from effective rates that include non-tariff barriers (currency manipulation, judicial actions), so the numbers can be set arbitrarily.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: we're going to have a minimum tariff of 10% on all countries
claims.claim: Tariff structure: autos 25%, country-specific reciprocal rates, and a minimum 10% on all countries, with China a separate negotiation.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: All these tariffs go into place. We'll put these charts up on April 9th country by country. And so we're going to hear all these ad hoc negotiations going on.
claims.claim: The announced tariff table is a starting point for ad hoc country-by-country negotiations (e.g. Vietnam) before April 9.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: we were at 77 billion last year and we end up at about 750 billion
claims.claim: Tariff revenue would rise from about 77bn to 750bn, above Navarro's 600bn estimate, but pharma and semiconductor exemptions probably bring it to about 600bn.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: there are very solid mathematical arguments why if you pull up the trade walls between multiple countries that you're going to hurt the efficiency of both of them um in the long run
claims.claim: Comparative advantage theory implies trade walls reduce efficiency in both countries in the long run.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: if you start that process today, it might take three years
claims.claim: Reshoring a factory from Asia takes years and costs more because US labor is not globally competitive, so tariffs cannot quickly shift production.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: which makes it very hard to allocate capex in any meaningful way whatsoever
claims.claim: Policy ambiguity (not knowing what tariffs apply in 3, 6, 12 months) makes capex allocation very hard; business abhors uncertainty and needs predictability to forecast NPV.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: They said things are slowing down in February and March because nobody knows what to do.
claims.claim: About 100 CEOs reported a slowdown in February-March from tariff uncertainty, and the Fed cut GDP and raised inflation and unemployment forecasts, raising recession odds.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: you're not going to hire a bunch of people, for example
claims.claim: Uncertainty cascades: firms pause hiring, which raises unemployment and eventually cuts consumer spending.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: three European contracts canled and one Asian contract cancelled because the countries were so upset with America
claims.claim: Retaliation effects: customers cancelling US vendors and China, Korea and Japan (and Europe) coordinating a response, shifting trade ties toward China.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: NASDAQ down peak to trough post Trump at almost 18%
claims.claim: After hours the Nasdaq was down nearly 18% peak to trough with many names down 40-50%, so fear is entering prices.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: I think we're going to land the plane here closer to three or 400 billion in tariffs, not 6 or 700 and certainly not a trillion in tariffs
claims.claim: Tariffs will settle closer to 300-400bn because the president wants deals and congressional Republicans, hearing from CEOs, constrain him (he cannot lose a vote on the reconciliation bill).

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: We're going to get a little bit more positive on the companies we like the best cuz we think some of this fear is now getting priced in.
claims.claim: After the selloff, add to favorite companies as fear is priced in, while watching exemptions (semis, pharma), country renegotiations and China.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: I don't think I see any clearing event here um for at least uh another 30 to 60 days.
claims.claim: No clearing event for tariffs for at least 30-60 days, so the market remains in the fog of war.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: the best opportunities to buy something are when people are a little fearful
claims.claim: The best purchase prices come when people are fearful, so one must take a leap of faith.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: it's imminent that he and she are going to have to talk and get a big trade deal done
claims.claim: A US-China trade deal is imminent because tariffs of this size on China are too large to hold.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: China has been supportive of open source for well over a decade now
claims.claim: Chinese support for open source is long-standing (not forced on DeepSeek), since open source removes IP-theft accusations.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: if they get in a position where they feel like they're behind the eightball. So they're not in a leadership position, they will embrace open source as an attempt to level the playing field.
claims.claim: Large companies use open source defensively when behind (Google/Kubernetes vs AWS, Android vs Apple, Meta/Llama), which commoditizes the leader's advantage.
claims.conditions: When a firm is not the market leader

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: Like it's just hyper competitive.
claims.claim: Open source creates the most fluid competition and lowest consumer prices versus proprietary code.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: it's been you know forked over 1500 times on their site
claims.claim: DeepSeek is prolific in enterprise (hosted by AWS and Google, forked 1500+ times), so Washington may act to limit its use.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: you have a window in the US right now where someone might move to go left of deepseek in terms of openness on one of their models
claims.claim: A short window exists for a US lab (Google or Meta; not Anthropic) to out-open DeepSeek, as an offensive or defensive move.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: we're excited to release a powerful new openweight language model with reasoning in the coming months
claims.claim: OpenAI committed to an open-weight reasoning model without Llama's 700M-user licensing cap, putting pressure on Meta before LlamaCon.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: What I'm hearing Bill is that it'll be a 400 billion parameter model.
claims.claim: Llama 4 is rumored to be a 400bn-parameter mixture-of-experts with a 10-million context window, launching before LlamaCon.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: they do not want to see a Huawei Deepseek Belt and Road either with chips or with open- source models
claims.claim: Washington wants the world to run on US compute and models (Llama, OpenAI) rather than DeepSeek on Huawei chips, tying to AI diffusion restrictions.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: kind of wiping out the business opportunity for other models to play on the API side if you make yours open
claims.claim: Open-sourcing a model protects the competitive flank like Google's Kubernetes move: others cannot make an API business, the model spreads globally, and compute is borne by users.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: the battleground bill is really going to be fought around products and services
claims.claim: Models are commoditizing; the contest is around products and services, with OpenAI focused on consumer (ChatGPT) and a leading enterprise business.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: Um because remember the consumerization of the enterprise. One of the fascinating things that's happening in the enterprise is these are all users of chat GPT.
claims.claim: ChatGPT's consumer base drives enterprise adoption (like iPhones displacing BlackBerry), with roughly 80-90% consumer share.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: market leaders never look cheap
claims.claim: Market leaders never look cheap (Google 2005, Meta IPO, Microsoft's round); judge by multiples relative to peers.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: So again you got OpenAI at 20 times, Anthropic at 50 times and then we had the merger of X and X.AI
claims.claim: OpenAI's roughly $300bn post-money is about 20x forward run-rate revenue (13bn year, 15-18bn exit) versus Anthropic at 50x and X/xAI at 80x.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: the headline numbers bigger than you know the peace meal when you start to unpack it which you know for better for worse from my position smells of being promotional
claims.claim: Mega-round headline numbers (Stargate, OpenAI) are bigger than the tranched reality and promotional, reflecting winner-take-all belief and a message to rivals.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: unit economics get postponed. You have to believe in the power law and the network effect.
claims.claim: Capital-intensive winner-take-all competition postpones unit economics, requiring belief in power laws; Bill compares it to Uber/Lyft and a sport of kings.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: they've said publicly they expect to lose, you know, five to seven billion this year
claims.claim: OpenAI expects 5-7bn of losses, with costs mostly compute rather than staff.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: I ran some loose numbers and I come up around 15 or 20 bucks a year for a non-paid user
claims.claim: Serving a free ChatGPT user costs roughly 15-20 dollars a year, which advertising or paid conversion may eventually cover.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: the winner does take all. The winner does take most.
claims.claim: Uber was called unprofitable in 2020 yet now makes about 6bn FCF, so losses along the way do not disprove winner-take-most dynamics.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: They crossed 500 million weekly average users of Chat GPT.
claims.claim: ChatGPT reached 20 million paid subscribers and 500 million weekly users, adding a million users in an hour.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: America's leading AI companies are all reporting that demand is off the charts. so much so that they're being forced to impose rate limits.
claims.claim: AI demand exceeds compute supply (rate limits, Sam asking for 100,000-GPU clusters), explaining the large raise and infrastructure build, and blocking product launches.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: the next big thing will first appear as a toy
claims.claim: Viral demand for image generation (anime photos) is a sign of consumer pull: the next big thing often first appears as a toy.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: what I see out of chat GPT reminds me a lot of kind of those winner take all consumer applications
claims.claim: ChatGPT's demand curves and cohort retention resemble early Google and Meta, so its consumer business will ultimately be valuable despite poor unit economics.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: I think most of Chat GPT users are using a model that's like a year old, right?
claims.claim: With more compute, upgraded models and pricing tiers would raise paid conversion above the roughly 4%, and a single smart model would replace the long model menu.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: either the user will pay or the end merchant will pay
claims.claim: In an agent world (booking hotels) value to users or merchants creates mixed models of ads, tiers and commissions.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: one of the reasons that Google is so susceptible to disruption is how they've maximized the revenue per visitor
claims.claim: Google's maximized revenue per visitor makes it vulnerable, since agent partners cannot pay fees close to what advertisers pay Google.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: they'll they'll pay 50 bucks instead of 20
claims.claim: Travel advertisers like Booking pay Google about 50 per 100-dollar room using LTV math, while an agent-underlying service could share at most about 10, a big disruption advantage for OpenAI.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: there's this acronym people are starting to use, MCP, that is a way for you to represent your service.
claims.claim: Open standards like MCP (started at Anthropic, now supported by OpenAI) let the most aggressive adopters define the agent ecosystem.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: I'm talking about like next 3 to 6 months could dictate who's standing on top of the hill 5 10 years from now
claims.claim: The next 3-6 months are a critical window, with executive shifts and anxiety at Google, Meta and Apple, ending 20 years of search paradigm dominance.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: They have Microsoft, Meta, now Google, OpenAI, Nvidia, Coher, Mistral.
claims.claim: CoreWeave diversified customers beyond Microsoft (Google deal on Nvidia Grace Blackwell), falling to about 37 around IPO then rising; it emerged as leading AI cloud.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: you can't control that thing. That's an external factor.
claims.claim: Do not wait for the market to be right before IPOing; IPO timing cannot be controlled.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: Their business model isn't fully unpacked because the capex is invested so far ahead of of the product.
claims.claim: CoreWeave's income statement is hard to read because capex precedes revenue and depreciation schedules are uncertain.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: the stripes of the world and and data bricks and others are choosing to delay being public and have massive access to private capital
claims.claim: Large private companies are delaying IPOs because of massive private capital access, offsetting the push for more public listings.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: cutting edge GPUs are going to be used for cutting edge training for the, you know, frontier models in that first two-year period. But all these things are going to continue to get used for inference.
claims.claim: GPUs keep value past the first two training years because they are reused for inference, so a two-year depreciation (implied by Jensen's 'chief revenue destroyer' remark) is too aggressive.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: They expect to pay back all the capex, opex, and GPUs in three years. And so, the fourth year, which is a four-year guaranteed contract, the fourth year is your profit margin, right?
claims.claim: CoreWeave contracts (four-year Microsoft, OpenAI, Google) repay capex, opex and GPUs in three years so year four is the margin; consensus EBIT around 25% gives no credit beyond contracts.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: OpenAI had just retired the V100s. That was a 2017 GPU. So that's like a 7-year life cycle
claims.claim: Evidence of long GPU lives: A100s (2020) still widely used and V100s retired after seven years; CUDA software updates improve GPUs over time.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: what inevitably happens is the earning power of that product drops over time
claims.claim: Depreciation should mirror the declining earning power of GPUs; six straight years is probably not the best fit (peers moved from four to six), the answer may lie in between.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: you have Nvidia trading at 19 times fully taxed earnings
claims.claim: Nvidia at 19x fully taxed earnings shows heavy skepticism about AI demand despite strong evidence.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: when the talking heads on CNBC and others are critical of a company because they trade below their IPO price, it's just such a wrong way to look
claims.claim: Trading below IPO price is a poor quality signal; Salesforce, Netflix, Amazon, Facebook, Palo Alto and others all broke issue.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: I think one of the reasons those highquality companies get priced to perfection is the founders are stronger minded and have more leverage
claims.claim: High-quality IPOs are priced to perfection because strong founders negotiate hard, which also explains post-IPO dips.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: the series C has a put right at like 3875. No doubt in my mind people wanted to make sure it priced above that
claims.claim: CoreWeave's series C put right at 38.75 likely influenced the IPO pricing at 40.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: they have to keep that owner ownership threshold under 20%
claims.claim: TikTok US rumored structure: new company with ByteDance under 20%, existing ByteDance shareholders (60% US investors) and about half new investors; the licence is to the algorithm.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: although it only trades at let's call it 300 billion most people think the fair value of this is closer to a trillion dollars are certainly to 800 billion
claims.claim: ByteDance trades near $300bn secondary but many see $800bn-1tn, so a TikTok deal unlocks hundreds of billions of venture DPI as a condition to take ByteDance out; TikTok US is about 10% of value.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: I'm hearing that the valuation for Tik Tok US could be pretty low, which I would expect
claims.claim: The TikTok US valuation may be low because Trump negotiates (sovereign wealth fund mention) and must clear Oracle audit of the algorithm.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: and the Chinese government could probably block the deal
claims.claim: After 54% tariffs, China could block the TikTok deal, so an announced deal is not done.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: Um I don't believe we're going to have 54% tariffs against China.
claims.claim: 54% tariffs on China will not stay because cooperation is too important (Ukraine, Middle East) and the president likes dealmaking with Xi.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: the most important thing that matters is USChina bilateral trade relations
claims.claim: US-China bilateral trade relations will dictate the direction of global and both countries' growth for the next few years.
